title: Eid al-Adha: sacrifice
hook: the sacrifice, the sharing, and what you'd give up for Allah
tomorrow: a king who could buy anything made his own armor. why?

segments.voice: This week walked the year. The book in the month. The last ten. Joy is worship. Carry Ramadan forward. The best ten. And yesterday, standing at home while the pilgrims stood on the plain. Then comes Eid.
screen: `STANDING AT HOME.` → `A WEEK THROUGH THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Ask someone what they'd give up for the person they love most, and the answers come fast: sleep, money, a weekend, a kidney. Ask what they'd give up for God, and people tend to go quiet. Eid al-Adha, the festival of the sacrifice, is built on that question. In the Qur'an, Abraham sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son. And he tells the son.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU GIVE UP?` → `THE FESTIVAL OF THE SACRIFICE.` → `ABRAHAM TELLS HIS SON.`

segments.voice: The son answers, in Pickthall's words: "O my father! Do that which thou art commanded." Both of them surrender. Then God calls out that the vision is fulfilled: "Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim." The passage doesn't name the son. Muslim commentators such as Ibn Kathir say Ishmael; Genesis, read by Jews and Christians, tells the test with Isaac. One story, kept in more than one house, with a name that differs. So what was really given? Not the son. The willingness. The Qur'an says it plainly about every Eid animal since: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." And the meat doesn't sit in one freezer. The Prophet ﷺ said of it: eat, feed others, and store some. The sacrifice turns into a shared table, and the question stays with whoever's holding the knife, or the grocery bag.
screen: `DO THAT WHICH THOU ART COMMANDED.` · `RANSOMED.` · `THE DEVOTION REACHES HIM.` · `EAT, FEED OTHERS, STORE SOME.` · then, large: `WHAT WOULD I GIVE?`

segments.voice: Look around for one thing you have more of than you need: food in the cupboard, a coat, an hour on Saturday. Decide who could have a share of it. Keep your eyes on that thing, or on that person in your mind, for the rest of the sit.
screen: `MORE THAN YOU NEED.` · `WHO GETS A SHARE?`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha: the festival of the sacrifice, remembering Abraham's test. The meat is shared; the devotion is what reaches God.
Your line: what would I give? Abraham was asked, and a ram came instead. The year's rhythm, complete.

howItsDone: On Eid al-Adha Muslims gather for the Eid prayer, and families who are able offer an animal in sacrifice, sharing the meat among the household, friends and people in need.
